join.e: From Middle English joinen, joynen, joignen, from Old French joindre, juindre, jungre, from Latin iungō (“join, yoke”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to join, unite”).
join.g: To connect or combine into one; to put together.

joint.e: From Middle English or following the -t model for forming a past participle.

joke.e: From Latin iocus (“joke, jest, pastime”), from Proto-Italic *jokos (“word, (playful?) saying”), from Proto-Indo-European *yokos (“word, utterance”).

jostle.e: Originally justle (“to have sex with”), formed from Middle English jousten, from the Old French joster (“to joust”), from Latin iuxtā (“next to”), from iungō (“join, connect”), equivalent to joust + -le.
jostle.g: To bump into or brush against while in motion; to push aside.

jot.e: Etymology 1, noun sense 3 (“brief and hurriedly written note”) is derived from the verb.
jot.g: The smallest letter or stroke of any writing; an iota.

journey.e: From Middle English journe, from Old French jornee, from Vulgar Latin *diurnāta, from Late Latin diurnum, from Latin diurnus, from diēs (“day”).
journey.g: A set amount of travelling, seen as a single unit; a discrete trip, a voyage.

journey.e: Reborrowing from French journée (day's activities), originally an unadapted borrowing from French journée, from Old French jornee, from Vulgar Latin *diurnāta.
journey.g: The total time spent melting and working one piece.

journeying.e: From Middle English journeyinge; equivalent to journey + -ing.

jowl.e: From Middle English jawle, chawl, chavel (“jaw, jawbone”), from Old English ċeafl (“jaw, cheek”), from Proto-West Germanic *kafl (“jaw, cheek”). The modern form (for expected chavel, chawl; still found dialectally) is influenced by jaw, which it is a partial doublet of.
jowl.g: The jaw, jawbone; especially one of the lateral parts of the mandible.

jowl.e: From Middle English cholle (“wattle, jowl”), from Old English ċeole (“throat”), from Proto-West Germanic *kelā, from Proto-Germanic *kelǭ (“gullet”) (compare Scots choll, West Frisian kiel, Dutch keel, German Kehle).
jowl.g: A fold of fatty flesh under the chin, around the cheeks, or lower jaw (as a dewlap, wattle, crop, or double chin).

joy.e: The interjection is from the noun.
joy.g: A feeling of extreme happiness or cheerfulness, especially related to the acquisition or expectation of something good.

joyfully.e: From Middle English joifulliche, joyfully, equivalent to joyful + -ly.

joyous.e: From Middle English joyous, joious, from Old French joieus, from joie + -eus.
